title.text:
Features and
choosing a model

objects.text: Which model should we recommend for predicting cooling load, and how do we explain the choice to someone who pays?

CML3112  |  Civil Engineering and Architecture  |  Week 11, class 4 of 4  |  Tuesday 24 November 2026, 11:00 to 14:00
KLAi  |  International University of East Africa  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to the last teaching class of the semester. Over three weeks you have built a model, judged it, and learned how to trust it. Today you compare several models and choose one. In real work you will have several candidate models for predicting cooling load, and you must choose one fairly and explain the choice to the client who pays for the cooling plant.

The ideas come first, then the lab, then the quiz for this block.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Build a new feature, test it with a feature ablation (ablation study) and say what the result shows
Compare five candidate models with the same protocol and choose one by the client’s limits on error and latency (model selection)
Choose a warning threshold by cost, open the test set once, and write a one-page decision memo

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can do three things. You can build a new feature from what you know about the building, test it with a feature ablation, also called an ablation study, and say what the result shows. You can compare five candidate models with the same protocol and choose one by the client’s limits on error and on prediction time, which is model selection, with the same rule that the project states as an instruction.

And you can choose a warning threshold by cost, open the test set once, and write the choice down in a one-page decision memo. The quiz for this block opens in the last 20 minutes of the class.

title.text:
Your three hours: models
and memo first, then the lab

objects.alt: The three hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Concepts first, with no laptops. Then the lab. The quiz opens in the last 20 minutes (open 24 hours).

slides.notes:
This is the last full class of the semester. The first part is concepts only, with no laptop: new features, two new models, a fair way to compare them, the client’s rule for choosing, and how to write the decision down. Then a break. Then the lab, where you build the comparison table on your own data and apply the rule.

The Block 2 quiz opens in the last 20 minutes of this class and stays open for 24 hours.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is overfitting, and how do we spot it?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Class 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is overfitting, and how do we spot it? Take a moment.

A good answer: The model fits noise in its training set, so it does very well on training rows and clearly worse on rows it has never seen. We spot it when the training error is small and the validation error is much bigger (a large generalisation gap).

Question two. What is K-fold cross-validation for? Say it to yourself first.

What I hope you said: K-fold cross-validation tests a model several times, each time holding out a different fold (part) of the training set, so we see how much the score moves.

Question three. What is data leakage? Write a word or two down.

The short answer: Information from held-out rows reaching the model while it learns. It makes the score too kind, so the model looks better than it is.

Keep these three in mind, because today builds on them.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Building a new feature (input variable) from existing features, using what you know about the building.
Also called an ablation study. Train with a feature and without it, on the same rows and metric, and compare the errors.
Linear regression with regularisation: an L2 penalty on large weights. Alpha is the regularisation strength.
k-nearest neighbours: average the targets of the k closest training rows. k is a hyperparameter (a setting chosen before training).
Prediction time (inference time): how long a trained model takes to give one prediction, in milliseconds (ms).

slides.notes:
Five words for today. Feature engineering means building a new feature from what you know about the building. A feature ablation, or ablation study, is a fair test of one change: train the model with the feature and without it, on the same rows, and compare the two errors.

Ridge regression is linear regression with regularisation, which is an L2 penalty on large weights. k-NN means k-nearest neighbours: predict from the k training rows closest to the new row. And latency, also called prediction time or inference time, is how long a trained model takes to give one prediction. A client cares about it as much as about the error.

title.text:
Class 3 in short: overfitting,
cross-validation and data leakage

rows.text: What is overfitting, and how do we spot it?
The model fits noise in its training set, so it does well on training rows but worse on new rows. We spot it by a large generalisation gap: small training error, much bigger validation error.
K-fold cross-validation tests a model several times. Each time a different fold (part) of the training set is held out for scoring, so we see how much the score moves.
Information from the held-out rows reaching the model while it learns, for example a mean worked out on all rows. The score looks too good.

objects.text: Check your own answers against these before we move on to today’s ideas.

slides.notes:
These are the three answers from Class 3, so that you can check yourself and revise from this slide later. Overfitting is a model that fits noise in its training set and so does worse on rows it has never seen. K-fold cross-validation tests a model several times, holding out a different fold each time.

Data leakage is information from the held-out rows reaching the model while it learns, which makes the score too kind. If one of your answers was different, say how, and we will look at it together. Which of the three do you find hardest to explain to a friend?

title.text:
In real work you compare several
models, choose one and explain why

objects.alt: In real work you compare several models, choose one and explain why

objects.text: The picture shows today’s four moves. Whoever pays for the building work wants the choice, the error in kW and the doubts on one page.

slides.notes:
Last class you learned how to trust one model. In a real project you rarely have one. You have several candidate models, and someone has to choose. That someone is you, and the person who pays, the client who pays for the cooling plant, will ask why. So today has four moves.

Build the candidate models. Test them fairly, with the same protocol and metrics. That is model comparison. Then choose by the client’s rule: keep the models within the limits on error and time, and take the lowest error. That is model selection. And write the choice on one page.

Which of those four do you think is hardest to do well, and why?

title.text:
A new feature can carry what
you know about the building

objects.alt: A new feature can carry what you know about the building

objects.text: Three training rows. The highlighted column is a new feature: load_pct times ambient_c.

runs.text: Feature engineering builds a new feature from existing ones. Here, hot air may change what a load costs.
A product of two features is an interaction feature. Row 1: 59.15 x 31.71 = 1875.6.

slides.notes:
The model sees only the columns in the table. If you know something about the building, you can hand it over as a new feature. This is called feature engineering. Take an idea from engineering sense. A building that is working hard in hot air may behave differently from what the two readings give separately.

So we build a column, load times ambient, and call it load_x_ambient. A column made by multiplying two features is called an interaction feature. Check row one by hand: 59.15 times 31.71 is 1875.6. Notice that this is only an idea. We have not yet shown that it helps.

title.text:
The new feature is a product, and the
extended model gets one more weight

objects.alt: The new feature is a product, and the extended model gets one more weight

rows.text: Intercept (bias): y-hat when all features are 0
Weights. In A, one more unit adds its weight

objects.text: Model B: x₃ moves with x₁, so one more percent of load adds b₁ + b₃ x₂ = 0.46 kW (row 1).

slides.notes:
The maths for the new feature. The product is x three equals x one times x two, where x one is load and x two is ambient temperature. Model A is the linear regression model you know, with an intercept of 1.49 and two weights. In model A, each weight is what one more unit of that feature adds while the other feature stays fixed: one more percent of load adds 0.45 kW.

Model B adds a weight b three for the product. Now x three moves whenever load moves, so the effect of one more percent of load is b one plus b three times x two, about 0.46 kW in row one. Work row one by hand with model B: the prediction is 51.8 kW and the actual value is 52.5.

Which weight in model B is the smallest?

title.text:
A feature ablation tests one change on its
own, with everything else kept the same

objects.alt: A feature ablation tests one change on its own, with everything else kept the same

objects.text: A feature ablation (ablation study): train with a feature and without it, then compare the errors.

runs.text: Red box: the new feature. MAE is the mean absolute error, the average size of the prediction error.
Same training and validation sets. Only the features differ.

slides.notes:
How do we find out whether a new feature helps?

We run a feature ablation, also called an ablation study. Build two versions of the model. They differ in one thing only, here the list of features. Both learn from the same 58 training rows, and both are scored on the same 15 validation rows with the same measure, MAE, the mean absolute error.

Model A with two features has an MAE of 0.74 kW. Model B with the extra feature has an MAE of 0.75. If anything else had changed as well, such as the rows or the measure, we could not say which change mattered. Which one is better, A or B?

title.text:
Removing ambient_c makes the error clearly
worse, and the new features do not help

objects.alt: Removing ambient_c makes the error clearly worse, and the new features do not help

objects.text: Each bar is the validation MAE of one version of the linear regression model. Shorter is better.

runs.text: Without ambient_c the error grows from 0.74 to 3.12 kW.
Adding load_x_ambient or load_squared (load times itself) changes it by almost nothing. Test every idea before you keep it.

slides.notes:
Four versions of the linear regression model, all scored on the same validation rows. Remove ambient_c and the error grows from 0.74 to 3.12 kW. So that feature matters. Add our new product column and the error goes from 0.74 to 0.75, a change of 0.005. Add the load squared and it is 0.75.

Those changes are tiny, and slightly the wrong way. A good idea from engineering sense did not help here. That is a normal result, and it is why we test every idea before we keep it. Would you keep the new feature?

title.text:
One-hot encoding turns a categorical feature into 0 and
1 columns, and equipment_id stays out of the features

objects.alt: One-hot encoding turns a categorical feature into 0 and 1 columns, and equipment_id stays out of the features

objects.text: One-hot encoding gives each category of a categorical feature its own column: 1 if the row is in it, 0 if not.

runs.text: The model trained on E1 to E4 has no is_E5 column, so E5 in these four columns is all zeros.
A column per known building says nothing about a new one, so equipment_id stays out of the features.

slides.notes:
A model needs numbers, so a categorical feature such as equipment_id has to be turned into numbers. One-hot encoding gives each group its own column, with a one where the row belongs and a zero elsewhere. Read a row across and you see a single one. That is a useful tool, and you will meet it again.

But look at the last row. A model trained on E1 to E4 has columns for those four only. E5 is a group it never saw, so if we squeeze E5 into those columns we get four zeros, which says nothing about E5. Our aim is a model that works on a building it has never met, so here we leave equipment_id out.

Where would a one-hot column be a good idea?

title.text:
Standardisation puts every
feature on the same ruler

objects.alt: Standardisation puts every feature on the same ruler

objects.text: Standardisation (scaling to z-scores): z = (value minus training mean) divided by training standard deviation.

runs.text: StandardScaler learns the mean and standard deviation (dividing by n) from the training set, then applies them to any rows. Ridge regression and k-NN need standardised features.

slides.notes:
You met standardisation, or scaling, in Class 2. We need it again today, because both new models are sensitive to units. Load runs from about 20 to 90, while ambient temperature runs over a much smaller range, and a distance would be dominated by load. Scaling fixes that.

Take the training mean of load, 59.9, and the standard deviation, 22.7. Row one has load 59.15, so its z-score, the standardised value, is 59.15 minus 59.9, divided by 22.7, which is -0.03. Remember the data leakage rule from Class 3: the mean and standard deviation come from the training rows only.

title.text:
Ridge regression adds an L2 penalty on large
weights, which can stop a flexible curve fitting noise

objects.alt: Ridge regression adds an L2 penalty on large weights, which can stop a flexible curve fitting noise

objects.text: Regularisation shrinks the weights (coefficients). Ridge regression adds an L2 penalty: alpha times the sum of squared weights.

runs.text: Dots: training rows. Curves: degree-6 fits of load_pct. A bigger alpha (the regularisation strength) gives a flatter curve.
Validation MAE (kW): 3.32 none, 3.05 alpha 1, 4.68 alpha 100. These errors belong to the degree-6 curve only.

slides.notes:
This is a flexible curve, a sixth-degree polynomial of load, through our training dots. With no penalty it can bend to follow noise. Regularisation means penalising large weights. Ridge regression uses an L2 penalty, and alpha is the regularisation strength. On the validation rows the error is 3.32 kW with no penalty, 3.05 with alpha 1, and 4.68 with alpha 100, which flattens the curve too much.

These curves are sixth-degree polynomials of load alone, so their alpha 1 error is a different model from the ridge regression on two features, with alpha 1, that you meet on the next slides. Do not compare the two numbers. Ridge is a preview. A little penalty helped here, and too much hurt.

title.text:
Ridge regression minimises squared
errors plus alpha times squared weights

objects.alt: Ridge regression minimises squared errors plus alpha times squared weights

rows.text: Loss function: the number made small
One value per choice of weights
Actual and predicted target of training row i (kW)
The p weights, one per feature. b₀ is not penalised
z₁ from load_pct, z₂ from ambient_c

slides.notes:
This is the ridge regression loss function, the number the computer tries to make small. The first part is the sum of the squared errors over the training rows, the same fit measure as before. The second part is the L2 penalty: alpha times the sum of the squared weights.

A big weight costs a lot, so the computer is pushed to keep the weights small. With alpha equal to zero there is no penalty and you get ordinary linear regression. The prediction below uses the standardised features, the z-scores z one and z two, so every weight is on the same ruler.

Why must the features be scaled before we penalise the weights?

title.text:
A bigger alpha shrinks the weights,
and here the validation error grows

rows.text: L2 penalty: alpha x sum of squared weights

objects.text: Ridge regression on two features. load_pct was standardised, so b₁ = 10.15 means: 22.7 more percent of load adds 10.15 kW. Alpha 1: loss 50.4 + 110.6 = 161.1. Its error 0.84 is not the degree-6 curve error.

slides.notes:
Now the real numbers, from your training rows, for linear regression with two features, here with an L2 penalty added. Each row is one value of alpha. With alpha equal to zero the weights are 10.15 and 3.44, and the squared errors add up to 48.3. As alpha grows, the weights shrink, to 8.58 and 2.75 at alpha ten, but the squared errors climb to 202.4.

Check alpha one by hand: 50.4 plus 110.6 gives a loss of about 161.1. The linear regression model has few weights to calm down, so here the penalty only costs us accuracy. It pays off when a model has many weights that chase noise.

title.text:
k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) predicts from
the k training rows most like the new row

objects.alt: k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) predicts from the k training rows most like the new row

objects.text: k-NN stands for k-nearest neighbours: find the k training rows closest to the new row and average their targets.

runs.text: Grey dots: training rows near the new row (zoomed in). Red dot: the new row, record 5. Gold dots: its 3 nearest neighbours, with their targets.
k = 3 is a hyperparameter (a setting chosen before training). Both axes are standardised.

slides.notes:
This picture shows k-nearest neighbours, or k-NN, a very different kind of model. Each grey dot is a training row near the new one, placed by its standardised load and standardised ambient temperature. The red dot is a new row. To predict, we find the three training rows closest to it, the gold dots, and average their targets: 44.3, 48.0 and 50.3.

The average is 47.5 kW, and the real value was 45.6. There are no coefficients to learn. The model simply remembers the training rows. Why did we standardise the features first?

title.text:
k-NN measures distance on the standardised
features, then averages the k nearest targets

objects.alt: k-NN measures distance on the standardised features, then averages the k nearest targets

rows.text: Distance from the new row to a training row
Standardised feature j: new row, training row
The k = 3 training rows with the smallest d

slides.notes:
Two formulas run the whole model. The first is the Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance on the picture. For each feature j, subtract the training row from the new row, square the gap, add the gaps up and take the square root. Work it for record 67, the nearest row.

The gap in load is 0.023, the gap in ambient is 0.127. Square both, add, take the root: 0.129. The second formula is the prediction. Take the k rows with the smallest distance, the set N k, and average their targets. The fourth row, record 81, is a little farther away, so it is left out. With k equal to three the average is 47.5 kW.

title.text:
The size of k matters: too small chases
noise, too large flattens the pattern

objects.alt: The size of k matters: too small chases noise, too large flattens the pattern

objects.text: k is a hyperparameter: a setting we choose before training. We try a few values and compare the validation MAE.

runs.text: Each bar is the k-NN validation MAE for one k. Shorter is better.
k = 1 copies one row, noise included. k = 20 averages so many rows that the pattern is lost.

slides.notes:
Same validation rows, three values of k. With k equal to one, the model copies its single nearest row, noise and all, and the error is 1.69 kW. With k equal to three it is 1.16, the best of the three. With k equal to twenty, it averages so many rows that it flattens the pattern, and the error is 3.72.

So k is a hyperparameter, chosen before training, and we choose it with the validation set. Ridge regression and k-NN are previews today. Support vector machines, random forests and boosting are planned for next semester. What would k equal to the whole training set predict?

title.text:
A fair model comparison keeps four
things the same for every model

objects.alt: A fair model comparison keeps four things the same for every model

objects.text: The picture shows the four rules of the protocol that every candidate model follows. Change one thing at a time: if two things change, you cannot say which one caused the difference.

slides.notes:
Now the rules for a fair race. Every candidate gets the same rows, the same split, the same measure and the same seed. The same rows means the same 58 training rows and the same 15 validation rows. The same split means whole equipment groups, with E6 held out.

The same metrics means MAE and RMSE in kW, and the same four-fold cross-validation. And the same seed means that wherever chance is involved, such as in the tree, we fix random_state at 17, so the result is repeatable. If one model got an easier test, the table would be a story about the test and not about the models.

Which of the four is easiest to forget?

title.text:
Every model also gets a four-fold cross-validated
mean and a sample standard deviation

objects.alt: Every model also gets a four-fold cross-validated mean and a sample standard deviation

rows.text: Model: one of the five candidates
Validation MAE on E5 (15 rows), as in Class 1
Fold: one held-out equipment group, E1 to E4
The model learns from the other three groups
MAE of model m on fold f
Mean and sample standard deviation: divide by k − 1 = 3

slides.notes:
This is how every row of the model comparison table is scored. The validation MAE is the one you know from Class 1, on the rows of group E5. The first formula repeats the MAE on four folds. In each fold one equipment group is held out, the model learns from the other three, and we average the four results.

The second is the sample standard deviation of the four fold errors. We divide by k minus one, here three, exactly as the project does; in Python that is np.std of the scores with ddof equal to 1. For linear regression the mean is 0.76 kW and the standard deviation 0.01.

title.text:
Model comparison table: five candidate
models on the same 15 validation rows

objects.text: Errors in kW; lower is better. A fold is one held-out group, E1 to E4. The tree keeps max_depth 4, as in Class 1. Class 3’s tuned depth (seed 17), 7, scores 2.62 kW.

slides.notes:
This is the model comparison table, the centre of today. Each row is one model. The first two numbers are the error on the same validation rows. The last three come from cross-validation on the training rows, where each equipment group takes a turn as the held-out group: the mean, the standard deviation and the range from the best fold to the worst.

The baseline model has an MAE of 9.69 kW. Linear regression, ridge regression and k-NN all do far better. The decision tree sits in between, even at the depth Class 3 tuned. Read the table slowly before we choose.

title.text:
Latency is the time a model takes to give one
prediction, and the client sets a limit on it

objects.alt: Latency is the time a model takes to give one prediction, and the client sets a limit on it

objects.text: Latency (prediction time, inference time) is how long a trained model takes to give one prediction, in milliseconds (ms).

runs.text: The red dashed line is the client’s limit, 50 ms. A red bar is over the limit.
k-NN is slow because it compares each new row with every training row. A control system that must answer within 50 ms cannot wait for it.

slides.notes:
So far we judged models on error alone. A client also cares about time. Latency, also called prediction time or inference time, is how long a trained model takes to give one prediction. For a building, a control system or an alarm may need an answer within a fraction of a second, so the client sets a limit: 50 milliseconds.

These numbers are invented for teaching: baseline 1, linear regression 3, tree 30. Ridge regression is as fast as linear regression. k-NN takes 60, because to predict one row it measures the distance to every training row. Which models pass the limit?

title.text:
Model selection follows the client’s rule: meet
both limits, then take the lowest validation MAE

objects.alt: Model selection follows the client’s rule: meet both limits, then take the lowest validation MAE

objects.text: The project states this rule too. The two limits are invented teaching numbers.

runs.text: Parsimony (prefer the simpler model) is why a client sets limits: good enough and fast beats slightly better and slow.
The test set never takes part. Cross-validation is reported, and it does not choose.

slides.notes:
We use one rule, the same one the project states. First, keep only the models whose validation MAE is at most the client’s limit, 2.0 kW. Second, keep only the models whose latency is at most 50 milliseconds. Third, of the models left, choose the one with the lowest validation MAE.

Fourth, if two tie, take the faster one, and if they still tie, the name that comes first in the alphabet. Parsimony is the reason the client sets limits at all: a model that is good enough, cheap and fast is worth more than one that is slightly better and slow. The test set never takes part in the choice.

title.text:
Linear regression meets both limits and has
the lowest validation MAE, so it is chosen

objects.text: Kept, sorted by validation MAE: linear regression: 0.74; ridge regression, alpha 1: 0.84. The first is chosen: linear regression. The test set takes no part.

slides.notes:
Now apply the rule by hand, one row at a time. The baseline model is fast but its error, 9.69 kW, is far over the limit of 2.0. The tree is fast enough at 30 milliseconds, and its error is 3.39. k-NN has an error of 1.16 but takes 60 milliseconds, over the limit.

That leaves linear regression and ridge regression, alpha 1. Sort them by validation MAE and take the first: linear regression, with 0.74 kW. In the lab you write this rule in a few lines of Python.

title.text:
The warning threshold is chosen by cost: 0.3
has the lowest cost on the validation rows

objects.text: Recall from Class 2. Warning: target at or above 54 kW. Invented costs, as in Class 2: FN 5, FP 1. The lowest cost wins; a tie takes the higher threshold.

slides.notes:
The client asks two questions, so the memo recommends two things: a model for the cooling load and a decision threshold for the warning. The threshold comes from Class 2. A missed warning, a false negative, costs 5, and a false alarm, a false positive, costs 1. These are invented teaching costs.

Cost equals five times FN plus FP. On the validation rows, threshold 0.3 has the lowest cost, 1. If two thresholds had the same cost, we would take the higher one, which raises fewer alarms. Check one row by hand.

title.text:
The comparison has four limits,
and you must say them out loud

objects.text: The data are synthetic, which means invented for teaching. Real building data would behave differently.
The validation set is one group, E5, with only 15 rows. A small gap between two models may be luck.
The test set is one group, E6, with 15 rows. Its score is one estimate, luckier or unluckier than the truth.
The client limits, the latencies, the thresholds and the costs are invented teaching numbers. A real client sets their own.

slides.notes:
Before we trust the table, four limits. First, these are synthetic teaching data, so real data would behave differently. Second, there are only 15 validation rows, from one equipment group, so a small gap between two models may be luck. Third, the test set is also one group, 15 rows, so its score is one estimate that could be luckier or unluckier than the truth.

Fourth, the limits, latencies and costs are invented for teaching. A good report says its limits out loud, because the person who pays will find them anyway. The project asks you to pick the true limits from a list.

title.text:
After the choice, group cross-validation
can hold out each of E1 to E5 in turn

objects.text: Linear regression on the 72 development rows with no missing value. E5 joins because the choice is made. In Python: np.std(folds, ddof=1).

slides.notes:
Once the model is chosen, the validation group has done its job, so it can join the cross-validation. The project does the same, with months as the groups. Here we hold out each of E1 to E5 in turn, five folds, trains linear regression on the other four groups and scores the held-out group.

It uses the rows with no missing value, so no imputation is needed inside the folds. The mean of the five fold errors is 0.68 kW. The sample standard deviation squares each fold’s gap from the mean, adds them, divides by four, and takes the square root: 0.10. More folds give a steadier picture of new equipment.

title.text:
The test set is opened once: refit the
chosen model on E1 to E5, then score E6

objects.alt: The test set is opened once: refit the chosen model on E1 to E5, then score E6

objects.text: The held-out test set (hold-out set, group E6) gives one honest score for the model and the decision threshold you chose.

runs.text: The refit on E1 to E5 is allowed: the choice is fixed, more rows make a better model, and E6 is still unseen.
The threshold is tested on E6 at the same time. Report the result and never change the choice.

slides.notes:
Here is the last step, and the one to treat most strictly. First you choose, using E1 to E4 to learn and E5 to score. E6 stays sealed. Then, once, you refit the chosen model on all 73 development rows, E1 to E5, and score it on E6.

Why is the refit allowed?

The choice is already made, so E5 cannot bias it any more. More rows give a better model. And E6 is still unseen. The warning threshold you chose is tested at the same moment. Think of an exam paper: if you read it and then revise, the mark no longer tells us what you know.

title.text:
A decision memo fits on one page, has seven
parts and recommends a model and a threshold

objects.alt: A decision memo fits on one page, has seven parts and recommends a model and a threshold

objects.text: A decision memo is a one-page note that lets the reader act. A related term is model card.

runs.text: The picture shows an example memo with its seven numbered parts, filled in with our numbers.
After the test set is opened once, its score joins the result line. The next step comes after the test: more real data.

slides.notes:
The last skill today is writing the choice down. A decision memo has seven parts, and it fits on one page. The question. The data. The models you tried. The result, with its unit. The limits. Your recommendation. And what to do next. The recommendation names two things: the model and the warning threshold.

The next step is what you would do after the test: collect real data from more buildings and check again with group cross-validation. The person who pays, the client who pays for the cooling plant, will read this and nothing else. Which part would you be most tempted to leave out?

title.text:
Read the recipe before you write it:
the client’s rule in four lines of Python

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: candidates is a list of records: one dictionary per model, with its name, validation_mae and latency_ms.
The list comprehension keeps only the records that meet both limits.
sorted with key=lambda sorts by validation MAE, then latency, then name, so a tie is broken the way the rule says.
The first record after sorting is the choice. If no model qualifies, the answer is None.

slides.notes:
Before the break, read the recipe you will use in the lab. Each candidate is a record, a dictionary with its name, its validation MAE and its latency. The first line is a list comprehension: it keeps each record that meets both limits. Then sorted orders the kept records.

The key is a small function, written with lambda, that gives three things to sort by: the error first, then the latency, then the name. The first record after sorting is the chosen model. If nothing qualifies, the answer is None. Can you read the four lines aloud in plain words?

title.text:

choose by the rule, test once, write it down

objects.text: A new feature is an idea: test it with a feature ablation.

Keep the models within the client’s limits on error and latency, then choose the lowest validation MAE.
Choose the warning threshold with the lowest cost.
Refit on E1 to E5, open the test set once, and write the memo.

slides.notes:
Let me gather today into five lines. A new feature is an idea, and we test it with a feature ablation before we keep it. A fair model comparison uses the same rows, the same split, the same metrics and the same seed, and reports the cross-validated mean with its standard deviation.

We choose by the client’s rule: meet both limits, then the lowest validation MAE. The warning threshold is the one with the lowest cost. Then we refit on E1 to E5, open the test set once, and write the memo. Say one of these lines to the person next to you in your own words, then we take the break.

title.text:
Four errors you will meet, what
they mean and what to do

rows.text: The new feature exists in one table only
Build it on both the training table and the validation table
A model received a missing value (NaN) and has no imputation step
Wrap the model with with_imputer(...) or add a SimpleImputer to the pipeline
IndexError: list index out of range
ranked is empty: no model met both client limits
Print kept and check the limits and the latency numbers
The cell that defines the helper function with_imputer has not been run
Run all cells from the top, in order

slides.notes:
Errors are normal, and reading them is a skill. These four are the ones you will most likely meet today. A key error on the new feature means you built it on the training table but not on the validation table, so build it on both. A value error about NaN means a model has no imputation step, so use with_imputer.

An index error in step eight means no model met both limits, so the ranked list is empty: print kept and check your limits. And a name error on with_imputer means you skipped the helper cell, so run all cells from the top. Read the last line of the error first.
